A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and matchable across renumbering, supporting a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original monosemanticity, concept-detection and steering experiments, including Tables 1–2, model comparisons and appendix ablations.

after.justification: V2 retains these experiments and adds original SAE-Bench, post-hoc finetuning, aggregation-sensitivity and qualitative comparison results.

M1.justification: Appendix I introduces an optional SVM-based FMS procedure using individual-feature classifiers and weight-ranked feature subsets. This alternative is outlined without experimental validation. The G-SAE architecture, conditioning loss and steering procedure remain unchanged; the finetuning study applies the existing method to pretrained weights.

E1.justification: RTP, Shakespeare, PII and their mixed-concept coverage are retained. V2 adds SAE-Bench evaluation but does not specify its evaluation data or task construction sufficiently to distinguish additional coverage from additional measurements within retained coverage. RedPajama is newly documented pretraining provenance for an already-used SAE checkpoint.

E2.justification: The main steering comparator set is unchanged. However, v2 Tables 10–12 add vanilla-SAE outputs and scores to the corresponding qualitative comparisons in v1 Tables 6–8. This expands comparator participation in those comparisons even though vanilla SAE was already evaluated elsewhere.

E3.justification: V2 adds SAE-Bench evaluation measures, pretrained-versus-finetuned controls, finetuning schedules using 25 or 100 epochs and learning rates of 1e-5 or 1e-6, and harmonic aggregation evaluation. It also changes the reported Shakespeare steering alpha from -0.2 to +0.2 for both SAEs and relabels the qualitative PII metric from F1 Score to Accuracy. These reporting revisions do not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained steering and feature-exclusion analyses, v2 adds finetuning sensitivity to learning rate and duration, arithmetic-versus-harmonic FMS sensitivity, and a USERNAME/EMAIL feature-isolation case study (Appendices H, J and K). Expanded qualitative comparisons also expose vanilla-SAE behavior alongside G-SAE.

E5.justification: V2 explicitly defines Figure 4 whiskers as the 10th and 90th percentiles; v1 leaves them unspecified. Existing standard-deviation curves and Mann–Whitney/RBC reporting remain. No additional seed counts, repeated-run counts or confidence-interval procedures are reported.

E6.justification: Tables 7–9 add substantial SAE-Bench, finetuning and harmonic-FMS results. For example, Table 8 reports privacy FMS@1 of 0.24 before finetuning and 0.33 after 100 epochs at 1e-5; Table 9 reports average G-SAE harmonic FMS@1 of 0.38. New vanilla-SAE qualitative scores and predictions are also supplied. Original main FMS and steering table numbers are retained.

T1.justification: Appendix I adds an SVM-specific formal construction, including feature capacity defined as the maximum individual-feature SVM accuracy and SVM-derived residual and cumulative accuracies. The original FMS equations, G-SAE losses, Gini derivation and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. No theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract and original FMS/G-SAE contributions remain. The conclusion now additionally claims that G-SAE can improve pretrained SAEs through post-hoc finetuning while preserving their general capabilities, broadening the method's claimed applicability and benefits.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive reasons for arithmetic aggregation, interprets the USERNAME/EMAIL example through FMS, and discusses reconstruction-versus-guidance tradeoffs. The conclusion proposes global disentanglement and adaptive loss weighting as remedies. Existing limitations concerning labeled data and residual concept overlap are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix H documents finetuning learning rates, epoch counts and approximate token costs relative to the checkpoint's 8.5-billion-token pretraining. The reproducibility statement replaces the anonymous code address with a named GitHub repository, also linked on the first page. The checklist still retains the anonymous address.

R1.justification: V2 adds the RedPajama reference to explain checkpoint provenance and gives the already-cited SAE-Bench a substantive evaluation role. The related-work discussion and positioning against existing interpretability and steering approaches otherwise remain essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section order are retained. V2 restructures and expands the conclusion, inserts appendix sections G–K, improves several captions and explanations, and updates affiliations, acknowledgements and the publication header. This is a localized revision rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: V2 adds capability, finetuning and aggregation tables, with main-text Table 2 summarizing part of Appendix Table 8. Three qualitative tables gain vanilla-SAE columns. Figures 1, 4 and 9 have revised labels, sizing, axes or whiskers; token-highlighted examples and the checklist are also reformatted. These substantially expand and revise the empirical presentation.

improvement.justification: The added finetuning, aggregation-sensitivity and baseline comparisons strengthen practical validation and scrutiny of FMS. Parameter corrections and clearer access information also help. However, capability-preservation claims exceed the new evidence: Table 8's privacy finetuning improves FMS@1 from 0.24 to 0.33 while CE score falls from 0.991 to 0.897 and MSE rises from 0.002 to 0.008. The added evidence improves the paper, but these unresolved tradeoffs limit the overall gain.
